Article
Enantioselective synthesis of mixed 3,3 0-bisindoles via a
phosphine-catalyzed umpolung c-addition of 3 0-indolyl-3-oxindoles
to allenoates
Yildiz Tasdan a, Guang-Jian Mei a,⇑, Yixin Lu a,b,c,⇑
a Department of Chemistry, National University of Singapore, Singapore 117543, Singapore
b Joint School of National University of Singapore and Tianjin University, International Campus of Tianjin University, Fuzhou 359297, China

abstract
An enantioselective umpolung c-addition reaction of 3 0 -indolyl-3-oxindoles to allenoates catalyzed by
amino acid-derived bifunctional phosphine catalysts has been developed. A wide range of chiral mixed
3,30 -bisindole scaffolds containing an all-carbon quaternary stereogenic center were obtained in high
yields and with excellent enantioselectivities. 3,3 0 -Bisindoles are valuable synthetic intermediates, the
employment of which led to formal total syntheses of (+)-Chimonanthine, (+)-Folicanthine and ( /C0)-
Calycanthine, as well as facile creation of useful pyrrolidinoindoline core structure.

1. Introduction
The 3,3 0-bisindole motif is an important structural unit that is
widely present in hexahydropyrroloindole (HPI) alkaloids ( Fig. 1 ),
a family of natural products possessing fascinating molecular
architectures and promising biological activity proﬁles [1–7].
Efﬁcient total syntheses of HPIs often rely on tactical synthetic
manipulations of key precursors/intermediates consisting of mixed
3,30-bisindole cores [8–14]. From a synthetic viewpoint, prepara-
tion of optically enriched mixed 3,3 0 -bisindole structures is a
long-standing and challenging task, especially in view of the pres-
ence of an all-carbon quaternary stereogenic center at the indole
C3-position [15–20]. In recent years, various synthetic strategies
have been developed for their asymmetric synthesis, including:
1,4-conjugate additions or epoxide-opening via Friedel-Crafts
reactions of indoles [21–24], Rh- or Ru-mediated multi-
component tandem reactions [25–27], as well as nucleophilic
substitutions of various 3-indolylmethanols and their structural
analogues [28–36]. Undoubtedly, given the extreme synthetic
value of the mixed 3,3 0-bisindole motifs, there still exists an urgent
need to devise efﬁcient approaches for their enantioselective
synthesis, especially those methods amenable for the preparation
of a broad spectrum of natural products.
To construct mixed 3,3 0-bisindoles containing a quaternary
stereogenic center, we envisioned that 3 0-indolyl-3-oxindoles
may be utilized as a starting material. In contrast to most afore-
mentioned literature approaches employing an advanced bisindole
intermediate containing a leaving group at the quaternary center,
there were only two reports to date using simple 3 0 -indolyl-3-
oxindole substrates via transition metal catalysis; Trost et al. [37]
disclosed a palladium-catalyzed asymmetric allylic alkylation with
allenes, and Arai et al. [38] documented a nickel-mediated 1,4-
conjugate addition to nitroethylene. We envisaged that the
employment of prochiral pronucleophilic 3 0-indolyl-3-oxindoles
in a phosphine-mediated catalytic umpolung c-addition reaction
may offer brand new synthetic perspectives – inversion of reactiv-
ities of substrates is especially noteworthy. The past decade has
seen marvelous advancement of asymmetric phosphine catalysis
[39–45], and in these endeavors, our group introduced a new
family of amino acid-based bifunctional phosphines and applied
them to a wide range of asymmetric transformations [46–53].
Considered to be one of the landmark discoveries in phosphine
catalysis, Trost and Lu’ disclosure [54,55] of phosphine-catalyzed
umpolung c-addition offers a new dimension in organic synthesis,
and not surprisingly, many excellent enantioselective umpolung
c-addition reactions have been uncovered over the time [56–68].
Among them, our group and the Zhao group [61,64,69] had demon-
strated that 3,3 0-disubstituted oxindoles could be easily accessed
by employing phosphine-catalyzed umpolung c-addition reaction.

In recent years, we have developed keen interests in devising new
catalytic methods for asymmetric construction of quaternary or
tetra-substituted stereogenic carbon centers [70–74]. Our
proposed strategy for the creation of chiral mixed 3,3 0-bisindole
scaffolds bearing a quaternary center via a phosphine-catalyzed
c-addition is illustrated in Scheme 1 . The 3 0-indolyl-3-oxindoles
appear to be ideal prochiral pronucleophiles, the hydrogen atom
at the oxindole 3-position is sufﬁciently acidic for basic
abstraction, thus allowing for subsequent reactions to take place.
The reactivity inversion of substrates is appealing: 3 0-indolyl-3-
oxindoles serve as a nucleophilic partner, as opposed to many
existing methods [28–36] employing leaving group-bearing 3,3 0 -
bisindoles as an electrophile. Moreover, in addition to allenoates,
other electrophilic partners could also be utilized, therefore greatly
broadening the reaction scope, making a diverse range of target
molecules synthetically accessible. The employment of 3 0-indolyl-
3-oxindoles with no leaving group also makes this approach more
attractive in a ‘‘green” perspective – the envisagedc-addition is an
atom-economical process [75,76]. Herein, we document a highly
enantioselective umpolung c-addition reaction of 3 0-indolyl-3-
oxindoles to allenoates, for the effective creation of chiral mixed
3,30-bisindole scaffolds, which are versatile synthetic intermedi-
ates for the total syntheses of HPI alkaloids.
2. Experimental
All chemicals which are commercially available were used
without further puriﬁcation. Thin-layer chromatography (TLC)
was performed on silica gel plates (60F-254) using UV-light (254
and 365 nm). Flash chromatography was conducted on silica gel
(200–300 mesh). 1H and 13C NMR spectra were recorded at ambi-
ent temperature in either CDCl 3 or CD 3CN or CD 2Cl2 on a Bruker
AMX500 (500 MHz) or AMX400 (400 MHz) spectrometer. Chemical
shifts were reported in parts per million (ppm). The data are
reported as follows: for 1H NMR, chemical shift in ppm from
tetramethylsilane with the solvent as internal standard (CDCl 3 d
7.26 ppm, CD 3CN d 1.94 ppm, CD 2Cl2 d 5.32 ppm), multiplicity
(s = singlet, d = doublet, t = triplet, q = quartet, m = multiplet or
overlap of non-equivalent resonances), integration; for 13CN M R ,
chemical shift in ppm from tetramethylsilane with the
solvent as internal indicator (CDCl 3 d 77.16 ppm, CD 3CN d
1.32–118.26 ppm, CD 2Cl2 d 53.84 ppm), multiplicity with respect
to protons . All high-resolution mass spectra were performed on
a Finnigan/MAT 95XL-T spectrometer to be given in m/z. Optical
rotations were measured using an Anton Paar MCP-100 digital
polarimeter. Enantiomeric excesses were determined by HPLC
analysis on a chiral stationary phase using CHIRALPAK /C210IE column
eluting with hexane/isopropanol mixtures as indicated.
Representative procedure for P1-catalyzed umpolung
c-addition of 3 0-indolyl-3-oxindoles to allenoates: to a stirring
anhydrous toluene (1 mL) solution of 3,3 0-indolyloxindoles 1
(1 equiv., 0.1 mmol) and catalyst P1 (0.2 equiv. 0.02 mmol,
9.5 mg) in an oven-dried reaction tube with a magnetic stir bar
at the indicated temperature was added allenoates 2 (1.2 equiv.,
0.12 mmol). The reaction mixture was stirred until the completion
of the reaction (2–48 h, monitored by thin-layer chromatography
TLC). The solvent was then removed under reduced pressure and
the residue was puriﬁed by ﬂash column chromatography on silica
gel, after the pretreatment of the silica with Et 3N (hexane:dichloro
methane = 5:1 to 3:1 with 2% Et 3N) to afford the product 3a/C0v.
3. Results and discussion
To initiate our investigation, the c-addition reaction of
30-indolyl-3-oxindole 1a to allenoate 2a was chosen as a model
reaction, and catalytic effects of a range of phosphines were
examined ( Table 1 ). L-Thr or L-Val-derived phosphine-carbamate
catalysts ( P1 to P4) displayed very good catalytic effects, furnish-
ing the desired c-addition product 3a in excellent yields and high
enantiomeric excesses ( Table 1 , entries 1–4). L-Thr-derived P5
bearing a sulfonamide moiety was also found to be a good catalyst
(Table 1 , entry 5), whereas the analogous L-Ser-derived P6 was a
poor catalyst ( Table 1 , entry 6). Subsequent examinations showed
that dipeptidic phosphine-sulfonamide ( P7), and phosphines with
an amide function ( P8 & P9) were all ineffective, yielding addition
products with low ee values ( Table 1 , entries 7–9). Thiourea-
containing P10 turned out to be a good catalyst, almost compara-
ble to the corresponding carbamate-bearing P4 (Table 1 , entry 10
vs. entry 4). Mono-functional, C 2-symmetric P11 was effective in

promoting the reaction, but ineffective in asymmetric induction
(entry 11). Accordingly, OTBS-L-Thr-based P1 was identiﬁed as
the optimal catalyst, and subsequent solvent screening conﬁrmed
that toluene is the solvent of choice ( Table 1 , entries 12–15). Fur-
ther enhancement was achieved by carrying out the reaction at
low temperatures ( Table 1 , entries 16–18). The effects of reducing
the catalyst loading and inclusion of different additives were also
explored ( Table 1 , entries 19–21). Under the optimized reaction
conditions, P1 effectively catalyzed the c-addition of 3 0-indolyl-
3-oxindole 1a to allenoate 2a, affording the desired product 3a in
98% yield and with 96% ee (Table 1 , entry 17).
With the optimized reaction conditions in hand, the substrate
scope of the reaction was investigated. In general, both oxindole
moieties ( 1) and allenoate structures ( 2) could be varied, and the
resulting mixed 3,3 0 -bisindoles 3 were attainable in mostly good
yields and with excellent enantioselectivities ( Scheme 2 ).
30-Indolyl-3-oxindole bearing either an N-benzyl group or an
N-methyl substituent gave equally good results ( 3a and 3b). The
reaction tolerated well the employment of allenoates 2 with differ-
ent ester groups ( 3c, 3d, and 3e). While 3 0-indolyl-3-oxindoles 1
with an electron-rich oxindole moiety worked very well for the
reaction (3f, 3g, and 3h), substrates bearing an electron-poor oxin-
dole were less efﬁciently converted; lower reaction temperatures
and longer reaction times were required for attaining desired
results ( 3i, 3j, and 3k).
Next, the reaction scope with regard to the indole moieties in
30-indolyl-3-oxindoles 1 was investigated ( Scheme 3). The reaction
was applicable to a wide range of 1 bearing different indole sub-
units, regardless of their electronic nature and substitution pat-
terns, and consistently high yields and excellent ee values were
attainable ( 3l to 3s). Furthermore, equally good results were
obtained when both oxindole and indole substructures in 1 were
varied at the same time ( 3t, 3u, and 3v).
We have not investigated the reaction mechanism in detail at
this stage but do believe that the reaction disclosed herein follows
the general mechanistic pathways described in the literature

[55,62]. A few experiments were performed to gain some
preliminary understanding of asymmetric induction. We prepared
30-indolyl-3-oxindoles 1 bearing different protective groups, i.e.,
benzyl and Boc, at the oxindole and indole nitrogen positions,
and studied their c-addition reactions to allenoate 2a under other-
wise identical conditions ( Scheme 4). Whereas employment of the
optimal substrate ( 1a) bearing two benzyl groups at both oxindole
and indole nitrogen atoms furnished 3a in 98% yield and 96% ee,
replacing either or both benzyl groups with Boc protection was
detrimental. Installing a Boc group at indole nitrogen position led
to the formation of 3a-I in 72% yield and 88% ee. Replacing the
oxindole benzyl with a Boc drastically lowered the enantioselectiv-
ity ( 3a-II, 59% yield and 41% ee), and the situation became worse
(3a-III, 53% yield and 25% ee) when both benzyl groups were
replaced. The above preliminary experimental ﬁndings suggest
that the hydrogen bonding interaction between the carbamate
NH of the catalyst and the oxindole enolate is crucial, which facil-
itates the overall transformation and is key to the asymmetric
induction. Different levels of disturbance to this vital hydrogen
bond result in respective reduced chemical yields and decreased
enantioselectivities (DFT calculations are on-going to understand
the origin of observed stereoselectivities).
The highly enantioselective umpolung
c-addition of 3 0 -indolyl-
3-oxindoles to allenoates disclosed herein readily creates optically
enriched mixed 3,3 0-bisindole scaffolds, which are highly valuable
synthetic intermediates, especially for the preparation of natural
products. As an illustration, the c-addition product 3a was oxi-
dized to bisoxindole 4 by treating with DMSO/HCl, and subsequent
allylation afforded bis-allylic 5 which contains two quaternary
stereogenic centers. Ozonolysis of 5, followed by reduction, then
furnished diol 6 (the absolute conﬁguration of compound 6 was
assigned based on X-ray crystallographic analysis (CCDC
1918373)), which can be converted to ( /C0)-Chimonanthine,
(/C0)-Folicanthine and and ( /C0)-Calycanthine following literature
procedures [11,77–80]. Alternatively, sequential dihydroxylation-
oxidation of 3a formed aldehyde 7, in which the indole core was
retained. Compound 7 then underwent a three-component reac-
tion with benzoyl hydrazine and TMSCN to afford a-aminonitirile
8 in a highly diastereoselective manner. Finally, hydrolysis and
reductive cyclization furnished compound 9, the core structure of
Gliocladin C and its related nature product family [81–87]
(Scheme 5 ).
4. Conclusion
In conclusion, we have developed a highly enantioselective
umpolung c-addition of 3 0-indolyl-3-oxindoles to allenoates,
catalyzed by amino acid-derived bifunctional phosphines. Notably,
this is the ﬁrst time that 3 0-indolyl-3-oxindoles are used as prochi-
ral pronucleophiles, and our strategy allows for facile creation of a
variety of quaternary carbon-containing mixed 3,3 0-bisindole
cores, which are structurally challenging and synthetically useful.

Synthetic values of c-addition products and the power of our
methodology are demonstrated in concise formal total syntheses
of ( /C0)-Chimonanthine, ( /C0)-Folicanthine and ( /C0)-Calycanthine, as
well as facile construction of core structure of pyrrolidinoinoline.
Currently, we are working towards developing more phosphine-
catalyzed asymmetric processes for the total syntheses of a broad
range of bisindoline alkaloids and their structural analogues, and
evaluating their biological activities.

Yildiz Tasdan graduated from Istanbul University, Fac-
ulty of Pharmacy with an MPharm degree in 2017. She
then went to Singapore to pursue her graduate studies
in Organic Chemistry under the supervision of Prof.
Yixin Lu at the National University of Singapore where
she obtained her M.Sc. degree in 2019. She is currently
preparing for her Ph.D. degree in Pharmaceutical Sci-
ences. Her primary research interest is synthetic
medicinal chemistry and modern drug discovery.
Guang-Jian Mei graduated from Zhengzhou University
in 2011 and received his Ph.D. degree in Organic
Chemistry under the supervision of Prof. Chuang-
Chuang Li from Peking University in 2016. Then he
joined the Jiangsu Normal University as an Associate
Professor. In 2018, he carried out his postdoctoral
research with Prof. Yixin Lu at National University of
Singapore. Now his research interest focuses on asym-
metric catalysis.
Yixin Lu obtained his Ph.D. degree in Organic Chemistry
from McGill University in 2000. He then carried out his
postdoctoral research with Peter W. Schiller at Clinical
Research Institute of Montreal, and subsequently
worked as an RCMS fellow with Ryoji Noyori at Nagoya
University. In September 2003, He started his indepen-
dent career and joined the National University of Sin-
gapore (NUS) where he is now a Full Professor.
Currently, he is holding Vice-Deanship at Faculty of
Science. His research focuses on asymmetric catalysis.
